title: Education in India
summary: Education is a deliberate, pre-designed learning experience meant to bring about pre-determined behavioural changes. Culture is the accumulated experience of earlier generations; education is the structured process of passing it on, and is itself shaped by culture, so the system of education changes along with culture.

Vedic period: gurus taught pupils who lived with them in the Gurukul (ashrama) in the guru–shishya parampara; education was the privilege of the upper castes; learning began with the Upanayana (sacred thread ceremony); it was oral, memorising the Vedas and Dharmashastras, later grammar, logic and metaphysics. According to the Maitrayani Upanishad supreme knowledge (gyan) results from learning (vidya), reflection (chintan) and austerity (tapas); self-education was the highest method (Bhrigu and Varuna in the Taittiriya Upanishad). Aim: the all-round development of the pupil's personality – education as inner growth and self-fulfilment; the mind itself was the primary subject. Mauryan and post-Mauryan period: guilds of merchants became centres of technical education (mining, metallurgy, carpentry, weaving, dyeing, astronomy for navigation); Ayurveda was systematised (Charaka for medicine, Sushruta for surgery; air, mucus and bile as the basis); Chanakya's Arthashastra describes princes' education after Upanayana (Vedas, logic, economics, politics); Ramayana's curriculum: Dhanurveda, Nitishastra, lore of elephants and chariots, painting and writing, jumping and swimming. Gupta period: Buddhist monasteries admitted students for ten years, had libraries and copied manuscripts, took students from China and South-East Asia, were maintained by grants from kings and the rich mercantile class (Fa-Hien studied at Pataliputra; other centres Varanasi, Mathura, Ujjain, Nasik); Nalanda University was known all over Asia (Vedanta, Puranas, epics, grammar, logic, astronomy, medicine; Sanskrit medium); the Jains used Adipurana and Yashastilaka in Sanskrit and later Prakrit and regional languages; books were palm-leaf granthas; mathas supported by Brahmins were parallel institutions. Post-Gupta: Harsha encouraged education in temples, monasteries and universities of Taxila, Ujjain, Gaya and Nalanda (Hiuen Tsang studied there; Shilabhadra was its head); in the 7th–8th centuries ghatikas (temple colleges) gave Brahmanical education in Sanskrit open only to the twice-born, which distanced common people. Subjects: metallurgy, baked bricks, glazing, mensuration, medicine (Takshila, Varanasi; Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita), mathematics (Aryabhatiya), astronomy (Surya Siddhanta). Languages: Sanskrit for Brahmanical education; Prakrit with Buddhism (Ashoka's edicts), Pali, Apabhramsha (Jain writers), Dravidian languages. Nalanda – post-graduate university for advanced study and research, famous for schools of discussion, with hostels; King Balaputradeva of Java built a temple for his students.

With the Delhi Sultanate the Islamic system (Abbasid tradition of Baghdad) was introduced; scholars came from Samarqand and other countries. Maktabs gave school education (run on public donations); madrasas gave higher education (maintained by rulers and nobles). Six types of institutions: by nobles and rulers; by scholars with state aid or donations; attached to mosques; attached to tombs; by individual scholars; attached to Sufi hospices. Famous madrasas: Muizzi, Nasiri and Firuzi in Delhi, Mahmud Gawan's at Bidar, Abul Fazl's at Fatehpur Sikri. Features: traditional in spirit and theological in content; the curriculum was divided into traditional sciences (Manqulat: tradition, law, history, literature) and rational sciences (Maqulat: logic, philosophy, medicine, mathematics, astronomy); traditional subjects dominated from Iltutmish till Sikandar Lodi, who invited Sheikh Abdullah and Sheikh Azizullah from Multan, who introduced philosophy and logic. Mughals: education through pathshalas, vidyapeeths, maktabs and madrasas; Akbar gave grants and started a college near the Jama Masjid; temples and mosques were centres of elementary education, teaching Sanskrit and Persian, supported by donations; no provision for women's education except at home for royal and rich families; Humayun introduced mathematics, astronomy and geography in Delhi madrasas; many Hindus learnt Persian and works were translated from Sanskrit to Persian; Akbar added accountancy, public administration and geometry, built a workshop near his palace, and his secular scientific system was disliked by the orthodox; memorising, discussing and writing out lessons were the method in madrasas; Akbar's Navratnas helped spread culture.

In the 18th century traditional centres such as Taxila, Nalanda, Vikramshila, Jagaddala, Vallabhi and Kanchi had disappeared; Hindus studied in their traditional institutions. The British first kept away from education; Warren Hastings started the Calcutta Madrasa (1781) for administrative reasons and Jonathan Duncan a Sanskrit college at Varanasi (1792); Christian missionaries opened elementary schools, including for untouchable castes. The Charter Act of 1813 set aside Rs one lakh for revival of literature, encouragement of learned natives and promotion of sciences; the Orientalist–Anglicist debate ended with Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's Resolution of 1835 (funds to promote European literature and sciences; English made the official language); Hardinge (1844) gave jobs to those with English education. Wood's Despatch of 1854 stressed diffusion of European arts, sciences, philosophy and literature through English or Indian languages, and proposed universities, grants-in-aid, teacher training and women's education; in 1857 the Universities of Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were set up (Punjab 1882, Allahabad 1887). Curzon's conference (1901) and the Indian Universities Act (1904) let universities undertake teaching, inspection of colleges and quality improvement. Colonial rule neglected mass education and made an urban elite as interpreters between ruler and ruled, stressing examinations; English education was uneven but produced political leaders and social reformers, created a common language link and brought ideas of freedom, democracy, equality and brotherhood.

To meet differing levels of development India needs an integrated programme of education; if education does not spread, economic inequality, regional imbalance and social injustice widen. The Kothari Commission (1964–66) called education the only instrument of peaceful social change; the Constitutional Amendment of 1976 put education in the concurrent list (centre and states share responsibility). Elementary education (classes I–VIII): Article 45 provides free and compulsory education up to 14; National Policy on Education 1986 thrust areas – universal access and enrolment, universal retention up to 14 and substantial improvement in quality; Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001). Secondary education: ages 14–18 (classes IX–XII); Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA) aims at universal access and quality at the secondary stage with a secondary school within 5 km and a higher secondary school within 7 km of every habitation; vocational education is a distinct stream at the senior secondary stage (about 5114 ITIs; National Skill Development Mission). Higher education: begins after class XII; development is uneven and few women, SC/ST students and rural youth reach it; gross enrolment ratio rose from 0.7% (1950–51) to 11% (2006–07). Adult education: age group 15–35; National Literacy Mission aims to impart functional literacy to 80 million; literacy rose from 18.3% (1951) to 74.0% (2011), male 82.14% and female 65.46%. Technical and vocational education: IITs and IIMs; brain drain. National Education Policy 1968 and 1986; Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district; Open and Distance Learning (NIOS, IGNOU). Right to Education: 86th Amendment (2002) made education a fundamental right; the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act was passed in April 2010 for ages 6–14; the school management committee or local authority identifies drop-outs and admits them in age-appropriate classes after special training.

objective: Answer in short phrases: How was the dispensing of education organised during the medieval period in India? Write two facts.
Makhtabs gave school education and madrasas gave higher education; they were supported by donations and rulers and nobles and followed a curriculum of traditional and rational sciences.

Explain any two characteristic features of Ghatikas in short phrases.
They were colleges attached to temples that gave Brahmanical education in Sanskrit, open only to the upper (twice-born) castes.
April 2026

Match two items given in Column A to Column B (the rest are distracters): Varanasi – Centre of learning; Yashastilaka – Jain literature; Upanayana – Maurya; Education – Architecture. Give two correct pairs.
Varanasi – centre of learning; Yashastilaka – Jain literature.

vsa: Explain the main changes which came in education during the medieval period.

The Islamic system was introduced with maktabs and madrasas under royal patronage; the curriculum had traditional and rational sciences; Akbar and Humayun added mathematics, geography, accountancy and administration; Persian was taught and works were translated from Sanskrit.
April 2026

or: Explain about the proliferation of Islamic institutions in India in the medieval period.
Maktabs for schools and madrasas for higher learning were set up by rulers and nobles, scholars, mosques, tombs and Sufi hospices; famous ones were Muizzi, Nasiri, Firuzi, Gawan's and Abul Fazl's.

vsa: Examine the spirit and content of Muslim education during the medieval period. Write any two points.

It was traditional in spirit and theological in content; lessons were memorised, discussed and written out; the curriculum had traditional (law, tradition, history, literature) and rational (logic, philosophy, medicine, mathematics, astronomy) sciences.
April 2026

or: How was the curriculum divided in two categories during the medieval period?
Into traditional sciences (Manqulat) and rational sciences (Maqulat).

vsa: Name two universities from ancient India, one located in Bihar and the other in the North-Western region.
Nalanda (Bihar) and Taxila (Takshashila) in the North-West.
October 2025
Examine the activities of the Indian Universities Act of 1904.
It enabled universities to undertake teaching (not only examinations), inspection of colleges and measures for qualitative improvement in higher education.
October 2025
Explain the significance of higher education in the development of India (any two points).

Higher education produces skilled manpower, leaders and researchers needed for scientific and industrial development and promotes personality, reasoning and learning; it is highly subsidised by the State.
April 2025

or: Explain any two challenges faced by higher education in India.
Uneven development and poor facilities in most colleges; low enrolment of the 18–20 age group, especially women, SC/ST and rural youth.

vsa: How does the Right to Education Act help in the spread of education in India?

It makes elementary education free and compulsory for children aged 6–14 in a neighbourhood school; local authorities identify drop-outs and admit them in age-appropriate classes with special training.
April 2025

or: Explain how school management or local authorities can help in implementing the RTE Act.
They identify drop-outs and out-of-school children above six years and admit them to classes appropriate to their age after special training.

vsa: Mention names of three countries/regions from which scholars were called to teach in Indian madrasas.
Arabia, Persia (Iran) and Central Asia (Samarqand).
April 2025
Why were guilds important in the Mauryan period for education?
They became centres of technical education fostering mining, metallurgy, carpentry, weaving and dyeing and patronised astronomy for navigation.
sa: Explain the importance of vocational education given at the senior secondary stage.

Vocational education is a distinct stream at the senior secondary stage that prepares students for various occupations, reduces unemployment and gives skills; ITIs train in 57 engineering and 50 non-engineering trades and the National Skill Development Mission supports it, though enrolment has remained marginal.

or: Explain any three developments in the Indian education system.

Free and compulsory education for 6–14 (RTE), Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and RMSA to universalise elementary and secondary education, and National Literacy Mission and open learning for adults and drop-outs.

sa: Mention any three features of the education system under the Mughals.

Education through pathshalas, vidyapeeths, makhtabs and madrasas; temples and mosques as centres of elementary education teaching Sanskrit and Persian, supported by donations; Akbar added accountancy, public administration and geometry, gave grants and built a workshop; no formal women's education.
Describe the education system under the Gupta period (Buddhist monasteries).

Buddhist monasteries admitted students for ten years, taught orally and later from texts, had libraries and copied manuscripts, took students from China and South-East Asia, were supported by kings and rich merchants, and Nalanda became famous all over Asia.
Write about the impact of English education.

English was encouraged to create clerks and babus; it became a common link language, brought ideas of freedom, democracy and equality that gave rise to national consciousness and produced leaders and reformers, but it was uneven and neglected mass education.
Explain the role of Wood's Despatch of 1854.

It stated the objective of spreading European arts, sciences, philosophy and literature through English or modern Indian languages and proposed universities in Bombay, Madras and Calcutta, grants-in-aid, teacher training and women's education; the universities were set up in 1857.
la: Briefly describe the development of education in ancient India.

In the Vedic period education was oral, in Gurukuls through the guru–shishya parampara, beginning with Upanayana and for the upper castes. Guilds became centres of technical education in the Mauryan period, and Ayurveda developed. Under the Guptas Buddhist monasteries (Nalanda) and Jain institutions flourished with grants from kings and merchants; under Harsha education was given in temples, monasteries and universities such as Taxila and Nalanda; ghatikas gave Brahmanical education in Sanskrit to the upper castes. The aim was the all-round development of personality and the training of the mind.
Discuss the steps taken in education with the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate and under the Mughals.

Under the Sultans Islamic education was introduced: makhtabs and madrasas with a traditional and rational curriculum; Sikandar Lodi invited Sheikh Abdullah and Azizullah to introduce philosophy and logic. Under the Mughals education spread through pathshalas, maktabs and madrasas; Humayun introduced mathematics, astronomy and geography; Akbar added accountancy, public administration and geometry, gave grants and tried a secular and scientific system; translations from Sanskrit to Persian were made; women were taught at home.
Elaborate the development of education from 1813 to 1904.

The Charter Act of 1813 set aside Rs one lakh for education. The Orientalist–Anglicist debate ended with Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's Resolution (1835): European literature and science, with English as the official language. Wood's Despatch (1854) proposed universities, grants-in-aid, teacher training and women's education; universities of Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were set up in 1857, Punjab (1882) and Allahabad (1887). Curzon's conference (1901) led to the Indian Universities Act of 1904.
Discuss the measures taken in independent India to spread education and eradicate illiteracy.

Education was made a concurrent subject (1976); the Constitution provides free and compulsory education to age 14; the National Policy on Education (1968, 1986) set thrust areas; Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001) and RMSA expanded elementary and secondary education; the 86th Amendment (2002) and the RTE Act (2010) made education a fundamental right for 6–14; the National Literacy Mission targets the 15–35 age group; Navodaya Vidyalayas, open and distance learning (NIOS, IGNOU) and vocational and technical institutions (ITIs, IITs, IIMs) were set up. Literacy rose from 18.3% (1951) to 74% (2011).
